facts.fact: Hyphessobrycon peugeoti was described in 2013 by Ingenito, Lima and Buckup in the journal Neotropical Ichthyology.
The holotype is MNRJ 38988. It comes from a stream at Cotriguaçu, Mato Grosso, on a tributary of the rio Juruena.
The species name honours the Peugeot family, who invented the Peugeot pepper-mill mechanism in 1842.
The family's business funded a carbon-sink reforestation project at fazenda São Nicolau, and that project led to the discovery of the species.
Because the name honours a family, the grammatically correct epithet would be 'peugeotorum'. The catalog keeps peugeoti as the valid name and says it need not be corrected.
The fish is also sold under the name Hyphessobrycon peugeotorum. After an objection to the change, it is again more often called H. peugeoti.
Adult males have a filament-like dorsal fin and a nearly straight anal-fin margin. Among its relatives, only H. loweae and H. heliacus share these traits.
In life it is red all over, which tells it apart from H. heliacus. H. heliacus is golden and has dark chevron-shaped marks along the midline.
It differs from H. loweae in two counts: 5 rows of scales between the dorsal-fin origin and the lateral line (H. loweae has 6–7), and 21–24 branched anal-fin rays (H. loweae has 17–21).
A freshly caught specimen had a dark red head top and back, a silvery body flushed carmine red, carmine-red fins and a dark blotch on the caudal peduncle.
The authors suggest it may form a natural group with H. loweae, H. heliacus, H. elachys and H. moniliger.
The measured specimens were 22.6–31.7 mm in standard length.
The species was described in 2013.
It is known only from tributaries of the middle rio Juruena, in the upper rio Tapajós basin, Mato Grosso State, Brazil.
Other known localities include a small stream on fazenda São Nicolau and the rio Juruena about 1 km below the mouth of the rio Arinos.
The video says it comes from a remote area of Mato Grosso, in the upper Tapajós basin (rio Juruena).
Specimens were caught in shallow water less than 1 m deep, early in the dry season.
The type locality was a swampy, deforested area beside a road detour, where grasses and small shrubs choked the flow.
One collecting stream had a sandy bottom, clear water and little aquatic vegetation.
Some paratypes came from a flooded area next to the rio Juruena.
The video says the habitat water is about 22–26 °C.
The video says it lives in small shallow streams and in swamps created by rainforest clearing.
Aquarium Glaser, a German wholesaler, offers captive-bred fish to the wholesale trade.
A UK retailer sells F1 captive-bred Peugeot tetras.
The video recommends a group of at least 10–12 fish in an aquarium of at least 80 L. It says bigger is better because some males can be territorial.
The video maker also says a well-planted tank of at least 100 L is needed, because the fish need swimming space.
A retailer says a tank of about 45–60 L suits a small group.
A retailer recommends 24–28 °C, pH about 5.5–7.0, and soft to moderately soft water.
The fish show more colour, including the black tail, under dim light. The video recommends floating plants.
Glaser found that only strong darkening of the tank brought out breeding colours. Warmer water, humic substances, live food and water changes did not.
In the video maker's tank, it took frozen food, flakes and granules straight away.
The video maker feeds frozen Artemia, Cyclops and Bosmina, and says live food is preferred and important for breeding.
It feeds near the surface and is a fast eater, so slow-feeding tankmates may go hungry.
A retailer describes it as an omnivore.
It is a peaceful schooling fish that can live with small peaceful fish such as dwarf cichlids and other tetras.
In the video maker's tank, adult Neocaridina shrimp were safe, but baby shrimp may be eaten.
Some males can be a little territorial.
Aquarium Glaser describes it as completely peaceful.

Adult males have a filamentous dorsal fin that reaches the base of the tail in fully grown fish. They also have a straight anal-fin margin with thickened rays and a stronger blotch on the caudal peduncle.
The video maker says females are paler, with less red and black, and lack the long dorsal fin. He estimates males are about 20% bigger.
Males in breeding colour develop a black tail fin. The tail fin is otherwise clear.
The video maker has not bred it in his aquarium yet, but saw males displaying and females following them into plants.
The video maker reports reading that, in aquaria, females lay several hundred eggs on plants or the substrate. Eggs hatch in 24–36 hours, and the fry swim freely after 3–4 days.
The video maker reports reading that adults should be separated from the eggs and fry.
